title: Revisiting Commercial Landings in the Kattegat and Skagerrak Between 1950 and 2023 Reveals a Severe and Sequential Depletion of the Entire Fish Community
content:
In this study, 74 years of landing statistics from the data-rich Skagerrak–Kattegat area of the eastern North Sea are examined. What can be described as a sequential depletion of species and unique subpopulations to the deterioration of the entire commercial fish fauna in one of the world's historically most productive seas is a clear warning to global fisheries.


ABSTRACT

Sustainable fisheries are integral to many policies, including food security and commitments to reverse biodiversity loss. Data deficiencies are, however, prevalent and hamper a comprehensive understanding of the long-term impacts of fishing on all exploited stocks within defined sea areas. Here we analyse 74 years of landing statistics (1950–2023) from the data-rich Skagerrak–Kattegat area of the eastern North Sea. The aim is to examine trends across all existing commercial fisheries on a fishing ground, including those for which stock assessments are often missing or more recently initiated. We find that total landings initially increased to a level around 450,000 t but have since then declined to less than 40,000. This corresponds to a reduction in fishery yields from 65 to 5.4 kg/ha. Sharp declines in landings can be observed across a range of commercial fish categories—from rarer fishing-sensitive species to main commercial species and industrial species destined for feed. In contrast, invertebrates show modest increases and today dominate landings, along with some flatfishes. This negative development is consistent with more detailed studies of individual species in the area. The overall catch level was maintained until the mid-1990s through time-limited exploitation of species or sub-stocks in the area, a pattern consistent with sequential depletion, after which total landings showed a sharp decline. What can be described as a collapse of the entire commercial fish fauna—occurring in one of the world's historically most productive seas, with access to extensive data and strict regulatory frameworks—serves as a clear warning to global fisheries in regions with poorer data availability and weaker regulations.
